reading.title: How Light and Stone Break Apart
reading.purpose: See how geologists and physicists study crystals, fractures, and bending light.
paras: Pick up a clear quartz crystal on a sunny trail and you are holding a natural geometry lesson. Inside a mineral, atoms line up in neat, repeating rows. When a rock suffers a sharp blow, a fracture, a clean crack running through the hard material, often follows those hidden atomic lines. Sometimes a tiny fragment snaps off the edge, revealing flat faces that shine in the sun.

Not every mineral breaks the same way. Thin sheets of mica are fragile, so delicate that a fingernail can peel or crumble them into flakes. Quartz is much tougher, yet even a huge boulder can split if water freezes inside a narrow seam. Scientists who study rocks sometimes dissect a core sample in a lab, slicing it apart carefully with a diamond saw to examine the thin layers inside.

Light behaves just as neatly when it enters glass or crystal. As a sunbeam crosses from air into a clear prism, the glass causes the rays to refract, bending their path so white light fans out into separate colors. In optics labs, researchers trace straight paths to see where two beams intersect, crossing at a single bright point on a sensor screen.

Math helps scientists describe every cut and angle they measure. A geologist might mark one narrow segment of a rock core, dividing a long cylinder into measured sections. On a circular mineral chart, each pie-shaped sector displays what fraction of a stone comes from quartz, feldspar, or iron. An engineer can even bisect a crystal lens, splitting it into two equal halves to test how cleanly each side bends light. Breaking and dividing materials carefully lets science see what stays hidden inside.

qs.q: In paragraph 3, the word "refract" most nearly means
choices: to bounce a beam straight back toward its source
to bend a ray of light as it enters a new material
to slice a thick rock core into thin flat sheets
to block all sunlight from reaching a lab sensor
qs.why: Paragraph 3 explains that glass causes rays to refract by "bending their path so white light fans out into separate colors."

qs.q: Which sentence explains how scientists inspect the hidden layers inside a rock core?
choices: Not every mineral breaks the same way.
Thin sheets of mica are fragile, so delicate that a fingernail can peel or crumble them into flakes.
Quartz is much tougher, yet even a huge boulder can split if water freezes inside a narrow seam.
Scientists who study rocks sometimes dissect a core sample in a lab, slicing it apart carefully with a diamond saw to examine the thin layers inside.
qs.why: This sentence describes the exact lab method: slicing a core sample with a diamond saw to study its inner layers.

ev.text: Scientists who study rocks sometimes dissect a core sample in a lab, slicing it apart carefully with a diamond saw to examine the thin layers inside.

qs.q: Why does an engineer bisect a crystal lens during a test?
choices: To divide it into two equal halves and check how each side bends light.
To melt the quartz and feldspar together into a single glowing boulder.
To keep freezing water from cracking the outside of the sensor screen.
To peel fragile sheets of mica away from the edges of the glass prism.
qs.why: Paragraph 4 states that an engineer can bisect a crystal lens by "splitting it into two equal halves to test how cleanly each side bends light."

qs.q: What is the main idea of this science reading?
choices: Mica is far more useful than quartz because it can be peeled easily by hand.
Diamond saws are too dangerous to use on clear crystals in a school classroom.
Carefully splitting, bending, and measuring materials helps scientists understand their structure.
Circular mineral charts are the only reliable way to record how light travels through air.
qs.why: Each paragraph shows how breaking, slicing, refracting, and measuring reveal the hidden geometry of stones and light.
